text: Took this course because I wanted to supplement my stats background with some machine learning know-how, but honestly, it was a letdown. The main issue was that it lacked hands-on practice, like in Module 5 where we were supposed to build a predictive model using scikit-learn, but it felt really rushed and poorly executed. Overall, I didn't feel like I gained any meaningful skills to enhance my education.

Three months into this Mobile Development course, I hit a wall - the instructor's explanation of iOS development in Module 7 was vague, to say the least. Honestly, I was expecting more depth, especially considering my background in software engineering. We used TensorFlow and React Native, but the assignments felt like repetitive exercises rather than meaningful projects. The final project, building a REST API, was underwhelming - it didn't challenge me like I'd hoped. What really stood out was the lack of advanced topics, like machine learning integration or security best practices. If I'm being real, I didn't learn anything significantly new, and the instructor's credibility was questionable. Took me about 3 weeks to realize this course wasn't going to enhance my skills like I wanted.

Took this course because I wanted to supplement my CS degree with some practical web dev skills, but honestly, it was a letdown. The biggest issue for me was Module 5's coverage of JavaScript, which felt rushed and left me with more questions than answers. Overall, I didn't feel like I gained much from this course, and it wasn't worth the time or money - definitely wouldn't recommend it to others looking to boost their coding skills.

Three months into this Web Development course, I hit a wall with Module 7 on advanced JavaScript - the instructor's explanation of async/await was unclear, and we didn't even touch on WebSockets or GraphQL. Honestly, I was expecting more advanced topics, like optimizing React performance or using TypeScript. That said, the course did cover some basics well, like the SQL tutorial in Module 3, but it felt too simplistic for someone with my experience. What really stood out was the lack of industry-relevant examples, like building a real-world REST API or using a modern frontend framework like Next.js - it made the course feel outdated, and I didn't gain any new insights to apply to my job as a professional upskiller.

Three months into this Design & Creative course, I hit a wall with Module 7 on UX design, which felt like a rehash of basics I'd already mastered in my 5-year career as a UI designer. Honestly, I was expecting more advanced topics, like accessibility design or AR/VR integration, but the instructor's explanation of design systems was overly simplistic. The thing is, I'd already worked with tools like Figma and Sketch, and the course didn't offer any new insights or techniques to enhance my skills. What really stood out was the lack of industry relevance - the final project, which involved building a portfolio, felt like a tedious exercise rather than a meaningful application of my skills. To be fair, I did appreciate the instructor's effort to provide feedback, but it wasn't enough to redeem the course's overall lack of depth and efficiency.

Three months into this web development course, I hit a wall - the lack of clear explanations in Module 7 on JavaScript fundamentals was staggering. Honestly, I spent more time Googling concepts than actually learning from the course materials. We used tools like Visual Studio Code and GitHub, but the instructor's explanation of async/await was vague at best. The final project, building a simple web scraper, was a letdown - it felt like a chore rather than a meaningful learning experience. To be fair, I was hoping this course would complement my university degree, but the content was disjointed and lacked cohesion. If I'm being real, the $500 price tag feels like a waste, considering the limited community support and lackluster instruction. What really stood out was how much I had to rely on external resources to fill in the gaps - not exactly what I expected from a paid course.

Honestly, I wasn't sure what to expect when I signed up for the “Advanced Marketing & Sales” track. I was a junior graphic designer trying to supplement my education, hoping the course would finally give me a foothold in client acquisition. The first two weeks felt like a blur of buzzwords—“growth hacking,” “conversion funnels”—and I kept wondering if this was just another sales pitch.

There was this one module, Module 4: Email Funnel Optimization, where Coach Maya walked us through a cold‑outreach assignment. I spent three sleepless nights drafting a sequence, only to get a generic template back with “good effort” and no real feedback. Halfway through, I realized the content was recycled from free blog posts, and the promised live Q&A turned into a pre‑recorded webinar.

By the time the final project—building a mock e‑commerce ad campaign—rolled around, I felt drained and honestly disappointed. Instead of confidence, I’m left questioning whether I wasted $400 and precious time. 1/5 stars.

After three weeks of wrestling with the onboarding quiz, I realized the promised “mobile mastery” was more hype than help. In Module 2 we were supposed to deep‑dive into Kotlin Coroutines, but the 12‑minute video barely scratched the surface and the code snippets were full of typos. The instructor’s “one‑liner to fix memory leaks” felt more like a gimmick than a real debugging technique, and when we hit Module 5 on Jetpack Compose animations, the walkthrough stopped halfway, leaving me to guess the rest. The capstone asked us to build a Flutter e‑commerce app, yet none of the prior lessons covered Flutter at all—so I spent an extra 4 hours Googling basics. As a senior product lead at a fintech, I needed advanced, industry‑relevant content and a credible mentor; this course delivered neither. Platform glitches, shallow content, and a cheap certificate make the 1‑star rating feel generous. If I’m being real, I won’t waste another dollar on this.

Three months into diving headfirst into Cloud Computing & DevOps, I hit a wall - literally, when I spent 2 hours on Module 5's AWS deployment section and still couldn't get it to work. Honestly, that's when it dawned on me that this course wasn't as engaging as I'd hoped. We used Docker, Kubernetes, and Terraform, which were cool, but the instructor's explanation of containerization felt rushed. The final project, building a scalable web app, was a letdown - it was too straightforward, and I didn't feel like I was learning anything new. To be fair, I was excited to learn about DevOps, but the course content was dry, and I found myself struggling to stay motivated. If I'm being real, I was looking for a more fun, hands-on experience, and this course just didn't deliver - hence the 1-star rating.

Three months into this web development course, I hit a wall - literally, I was stuck on Module 4's JavaScript exercises for what felt like an eternity. Honestly, the instructor's explanation of closures was confusing, and we didn't even get to use cool tools like React or Django until the very end. What really stood out was how dry the content was, I mean, who thought it was a good idea to dedicate an entire module to CSS grid without any interactive examples? Took me about 3 weeks to trudge through that part. If I'm being real, the course just didn't keep me engaged - I was doing this for fun, but it felt like a chore. The final project, building a simple to-do list app, was kinda cool, but by that point, I was already checked out.
